IMPORTATION OF U.S. CORN-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon), the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the failure of the government to take appropriate measures to protect the Canadian farmers by preventing the dumping of American com in Canada at fire sale prices, as well as the government's failure to take action to stabilize prices for Canadian corn producers, resulting in the disastrous collapse of the Canadian corn market.
If Your Honour finds some difficulty in determining the urgency of the matter, I am prepared to debate it at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: IMPORTATION OF U.S. CORN-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order, please. As the hon. member realizes, it is not the urgency of the matter that most concerns the Chair at the moment but the urgency of debate on the matter. I would invite the hon. member to address the house on this limited aspect of the matter.

subtopic: IMPORTATION OF U.S. CORN-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The urgency of debate arises from the subject matter of the motion, which relates to antidumping provisions. I am firmly convinced there is no way in which the question of anti-dumping provisions can be debated at this time. It is urgent that the debate take place now because measures would have to be implemented immediately in order to save for the farmers any substantial part of the 1968 market.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
A further factor relating to urgency of debate is the fact that only this morning was it fully apparent that the government had absolutely nothing to offer to relieve the disastrous situation in which the com producers find themselves. Up until yesterday the
minister had left the impression that some kind of action would be taken by the government.
That suggestion was completely dissipated today. Now that we know nothing is being done to deal in a practical way with the situation resulting from the dumping of cheap United States corn at fire sale prices, it is up to this parliament to act. That is why the farmers have arrived here today to bring their case to parliament, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, they have a right to have their case heard. On another similar occasion last spring the farmers found the doors of parliament locked in their faces, the only time in the history of this nation that this has happened. I maintain that this is an urgent and an important case nationally, and if parliament is to be once again closed off to the farmers, where are they to turn?
A great principle is involved here, and surely it must be admitted that it is not every day that the deliberations of this chamber are interrupted by the primary producers of this country seeking justice from this house; because that is all the farmers are asking. There is no other way in which this matter can be dealt with, no other way in which the farmers of this country can find justice other than to ask this house to interrupt its deliberations at this time to deal with the question of according them the opportunity to sell their products without interference.
For my part I do not feel the least embarrassment in asking this house to deal with this question now, because it is a question basic to our institutions and to the survival in this nation of the important producing industries which are at the very base and foundation of our economy. I am proud to make this request on behalf of the farmers of Canada. I wish the Minister of Agriculture would join me in my view that parliament would be fulfilling its functions nobly if it interrupted its proceedings now to deal with this very real, urgent and pressing grievance of the farmers of Canada at this time.

item is about $1.22 per bushel. If the price continues to fall at this rate, and if the debate takes place only in three or four weeks, then the farmers will be ruined. There is therefore urgency of debate in connection with this matter now.

I agree that the matter needs immediate attention, but I suggest to Your Honour that immediate attention has been given and that action has already been taken. Paragraph 3 of citation 100 deals with urgency, and this means not urgency of the matter but urgency of debate. I should like to couple that with part of paragraph 8 of citation 100, which quotes the Speaker of the British House of Commons as saying in part:
What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs. That is not the purpose of the standing order-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Will the minister give a report to the house on his meetings with the delegation of Ontario farmers this morning; and will he state what undertakings, if any, he gave to those farmers on action with respect to the grave problems faced by the Ontario corn growers?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETINGS WITH ONTARIO FARMERS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, but under the rules I will not be able to make as long a reply as I would like. Just a few minutes ago we had a very satisfactory meeting with the Ontario corn producers who are here protesting against the decline in the prices received for their corn in Ontario. I think it was an exchange of views that was useful both to me, as the representative of the government and to the members of the union.
I gave an undertaking that we had initiated action, and that we were going to pursue it immediately, to make sure there was no corn coming into Canada below the United States support level. At what price that level is, is something we intend to argue. It is not all that clear because of the very complex way in which the United States pays subsidies to its corn producers. subtopic: STATEMENT ON 1968 BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members already know that 1968 will be a record year for housing in Canada.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON 1968 BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON 1968 BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
The original estimate of 175,000 new housing starts in all areas in Canada is now virtually assured, and there is every prospect that the final figure will be close to 185,000. However, distribution of new housing starts as between rental accommodation and single family dwellings for home ownership continues to cause concern. Multiple dwelling starts for the first nine months are 26 per cent higher than the comparable total for 1967, whereas the rate for single family dwellings is 8.4 per cent less than 1967.
The original estimate of housing starts for this year was based on the expectation that
100.000	multiple housing units for rental purposes and 75,000 single family dwellings for home ownership would be started in 1968. There would appear to be a very real possibility that single family dwellings started will fall short of 75,000 units and that multiple housing for rental purposes may exceed 100,000 housing units.
In order to alleviate the shortage of family accommodation, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been authorized to make, from within its capital budget, $170 million available for commitments for home ownership dwellings during the balance of the year. This represents 9,000 units of new construction in the form of single family dwellings and condominium together with 2,000 loans on existing dwellings. I would also point out that standing order 39(5) of the rules of this house provides that:
Before the orders of the day are proceeded with, questions on matters of urgency may be addressed orally to ministers of the crown-
This statement was included in a recommendation of the procedure committee which was adopted by the house unanimously, I believe. There is no suggestion that questions should be asked only of some ministers of the crown. There is no suggestion that they be limited to such ministers of the crown as the government or the right hon. gentleman see fit to designate to be in the house. The recommendation covered all ministers of the crown.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I submit in as strong terms as I can that this action of the government, all the more flagrant because it goes in the face of the very reasonable and moderate criticism of this proposal when it was first broached, and in view of the fact that a standing committee has now been established with terms of reference requiring the committee to pay attention to this matter, is a very contrived contempt of the House of Commons.
The rights of the members of this house under standing order 39 go a step further. They have now been given the right, when Your Honour for reasons that you think are proper rules that a question is not urgent or when hon. members are not satisfied with the answer, to give appropriate notice and debate the matter, and this plan cuts down that right.
While I base my submission on the statement of the Prime Minister and on the absence from the house of ministers who should
Inquiries of the Ministry be here to answer these questions, I also base it on a letter that was sent to all members of the House of Commons, and which I assume is public property, by the President of the Privy Council. Dated yesterday it says:
On Wednesday, September 25, the Prime Minister asked the house for co-operation in an experiment in relation to the attendance by ministers during the daily question period. I am enclosing a copy of the roster.
On examining the roster, Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that this is the day the Minister of Agriculture will not be in the house. The whole farcical nature of this experiment is shown by the fact that the minister is not so obviously engaged on business, because when the application under standing order 26 was made he came into the chamber. This arrangement is contrived and continues to be contrived, I say, in complete contempt of the house and parliament.
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, the second paragraph reads as follows:
This roster is based chiefly on the cabinet obligations of the ministers. Naturally, from time to time ministers will have to be away because of other public responsibilities or illness. It is not suggested that questions should be delayed in such instances; rather, they could be addressed to the Acting Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary.
The only inference that hon. members can derive from that letter is that when, in response to the dictates of the Prime Minister, ministers are not in the house, questions asked of them by hon. members will not be answered but will be disregarded. No attention will be paid to them at all. I think that is quite plain, sir. What the President of the Privy Council is saying in this second paragraph of the letter is that where the minister is away on legitimate business questions can be directed to parliamentary secretaries or the acting minister. He is saying: When a minister is away because the Prime Minister has said he is not to be here, no attention will be paid to questions.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that those of us who have had the opportunity of seeing the extent to which the question period in the United Kingdom has deteriorated to the point that it is useless see in this practice a very serious and retrograde step. I suggest to the government, to the right hon. gentleman and to the President of the Privy Council that if they are seriously interested in saving time and in the expeditious handling of the business of the house, then the one minute or so spent in asking a question and giving an answer could well save a great deal of time later when a member, frustrated in his desire to obtain

In the past, Mr. Speaker, when one minister was away for a period, say at the United Nations, it was possible that the opposition could be stonewalled. A government could say that it would not answer a certain question until the minister returned and that he would answer the question in ten days' or a fortnight's time. We believe that this present arrangement will put the government under an obligation to have somebody here to answer questions in specific departmental areas. If the minister himself cannot be here on a day when he is supposed to be here, then he will be replaced by the acting minister or the second acting minister, by his parliamentary secretary or by the Prime Minister. Someone will have to attempt to answer, and the departments of the absent ministers will be able to brief the acting minister. We hope that this will be to the advantage of the opposition. If it is not to the advantage of parliament we shall discontinue the system.

With the greatest of respect to the statements made by the Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council, may I say I consider they are trying to put something over on parliament and the Canadian people. I wish to come to grips with the argument advanced by the President of the Privy Council. Let me read the standing order. It says:
Before orders of the day are proceeded with, questions on matters of urgency may be addressed orally to ministers of the crown-
Nowhere do we find that only some ministers can be questioned on any day. The word "all" is not there, but nowhere does it say that only some ministers may be questioned. The idea is that members of the opposition can question the executive of this country whose function it is to govern, and I think this is where the President of the Privy Council confuses the functions of government with those of parliament.
Let us take a look at the history which led up to this occasion. The government asked members of the opposition to acquiesce in the setting up of a committee to inquire into the various rules which govern the procedures of this house. The opposition worked together with the government in a co-operative manner and a committee was set up to look into the very procedures we are now discussing. The next day the Prime Minister came into the house and unilaterally, without taking parliament into his confidence or placing the question before the committee, made a decision by saying in effect: We are the masters of this house and we intend to implement a rule whether you like it or not.
The Prime Minister put forward a foolish argument when he referred to the absence of some members of the opposition from this chamber. The fact is that it is the function of the government to govern, and it is the duty of ministers to be here and ready to answer questions so that facts may be obtained by members of the opposition. It seems to me he is confusing the roles of the government and of the opposition.

Before you rise, Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will allow me to make a fundamental point, one which those sitting on the back benches opposite should heed. There are two occasions when a backbencher can stand up in this house and confront a minister. One is during the question period, the other is when the estimates of a department are before the house in committee and it is possible to comment on particular points affecting a constituency in the expectation of a reply. I only wish backbenchers across the way would appreciate the fundamental principle involved here. It does not affect the opposition alone.
So far as the efficiency of this house is concerned, how efficient will the house be when I stand up as a backbencher and direct a question to the Minister of Transport which, it turns out, falls within the responsibility of one of his colleagues? We had an instance today. A question was asked of one minister and he replied "No, that is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources." Every day, because of the interlocking of departments, one minister hands over questions to another. The Postmaster General, I suppose, is going to be the minister of communications, of the post office, and perhaps of satellites, but there will be conflict with the Department of Transport.
Instead of an efficient house and a shorter question period this proposal will complicate the problem. The question period has not been the problem in this house during my experience, which is the same in time as that of the Leader of the Opposition, two and a half years. In passing may I say that the class of '65 on the government side has gone ahead a heck of a lot faster than the class of '65 on this side.

There is one argument which shows there is a redeeming feature about the parliamentary system and affects the relative power of the executive and private members, under our system, unlike any other, there is provision for members of the executive being held to daily account. This is done through the question period, at which time the tradition and practice have been that members of the cabinet present themselves for interrogation and to supply information. It is not just that they are expected to do so; this is an old practice that goes back over the centuries. Just as the right hon. member for Prince Albert indicated earlier today, I think the indication the Prime Minister has given that this practice will be impinged upon simply for the convenience of the executive will be very much to the detriment of parliament as a whole.

speakeroldname: Hon. Olio E. Lang (Minister without Portfolio):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT, RATE OF CALCULATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a great pleasure for me to rise in this house today to speak on a resolution which is of such importance to prairie farmers in particular. The amendments which this resolution proposes are very important at the present time, and I hope that everyone in the house will agree fairly quickly that this is indeed the case.
Perhaps it would be appropriate for me at this stage to touch briefly upon some of the history of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and to describe some of its uses in the past. This act was proclaimed on November 25, 1957 and through it cash has been advanced interest free to grain producers in western Canada against the security of threshed farm-stored grain. This has meant that producers have been able to receive cash for their products when there has been a delay in delivering to country elevators. From the time the program began, approximately 21 per cent of the eligible farmers have each year taken advantage of this act. The total cash advances over the nearly 11 year period have amounted to about $450 million. Each year on an average approximately $40 million has been advanced in this fashion.

October 4, 1968
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
In the 1967-68 crop year the total exceeded $47 million in advances to 45,811 producers. The recovery rate has been particularly good over the period this scheme has been in effect. Something in excess of 99.5 per cent of all advances has been recovered. In this scheme the government has borne the interest charges involved, and the total interest to the end of July of 1968 has amounted to $7.5 million. The government's share of default has come to a total of $49,845. Both figures cover the 11 year period during which the act has been in effect.
It is interesting to note that it has been generally the smaller producer who has benefited from the act. In only one year, the last year, has the average advance for all producers exceeded $1,000. In this last year the figure was $1,032.
I would now like to touch briefly on the main features of the proposed amendments to the act. The maximum advance under the act will be increased from $3,000 to $6,000. Comparatively few producers have sufficient acreage to allow them to benefit from this increase alone, and to ensure that the smaller producers will benefit from the act the rate of advance per bushel is to be dealt with. This will change the present rates so that in place of 50 cents per bushel for wheat an advance of $1 per bushel will be available. For oats, the figure of 20 cents will be changed to 40 cents per bushel, and for barley 35 cents will become 70 cents. With these new rates, these producers will be able to obtain double the amount they could have obtained under the existing act.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
In a subsidiary change, exceptions relating to the unit quota or the initial quota will be removed from the act. The unit quota, of course, allows each producer, regardless of his acreage, to make a specific initial delivery of grain. In the existing act, grain which a farmer has on hand to fill his unit quota is not counted in determining his eligibility for an advance. In the new act, the distinction between unit and regular quotas will be removed. Because no change is contemplated in the schedule for repayment of advances, the burden of repayment relative to the advance will be lessened. For various reasons, the unit delivery will also then be counted for repayment purposes, as it is for eligibility. I think this is a most important point, that there is no change in the schedule for repayment, and I emphasize it even though it is clearly not an amendment to the act. Because 
of the increase in advances, the lack of any change in the repayment schedule will be of distinct advantage to the producer.
I want to assure hon. members that in the proposed amendments there will be provision for those producers who may already have applied for an advance in this crop year. These producers will be able to apply for additional advances which will put them in the same position as a fellow producer who has not yet made use of the act. Other amendments of a more routine nature will not be enlarged upon by me here. Of course, there will be opportunities to discuss them at a later stage. They are generally designed to facilitate administration of the act in the circumstances of the larger advances which I have described.
The Canadian Wheat Board administers this act on behalf of the government and the elevator companies and their agents extend the advances to the individual producers on application. The act has functioned very well these past years. I want to express the appreciation of the government to the Canadian Wheat Board and to the various elevator companies for the effective manner in which this act has been administered.
The grain producers, too, deserve credit for their co-operation and a particular word of praise for their repayment record. This does not surprise those of us who know the character of the Canadian farmer, but I draw it to the attention of less fortunate members. I look forward, Mr. Chairman, to the approval of these amendments so that this act, so important to the farmers, can be brought more into line with present conditions.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to say a few words at the resolution stage of this cash advance legislation, I cannot help but note the minister's closing words. He said that these amendments would update the legislation and keep it in step with conditions. It is sad that western farmers have to have this legislation to double the advances that may be made. It is known, of course, that their costs have doubled. It is a sad thing, really, that very little has been done about this, but the farmer will be given a larger cash advance on his grain. It is a sad thing that something more has not been done to help reduce the costs or alleviate the load these costs impose on the farmer.
I cannot help but think back to the introduction of this act in 1957. We western farmers argued for something like this as far back as the fifties. The former deputy minister of trade and commerce said it could not be done; it would be impossible to administer. The statement of the deputy minister of that day is in line with the statement the Minister of Agriculture made today when he told the corn farmers of southern Ontario it was impossible to bring their product under the stabilization measure. As I say, the deputy minister of trade and commerce said at that time it was impossible to administer legislation of this type, but 11 years later the measure has been proven to be feasible.
I am glad that the present minister of external affairs, who at that time was deputy minister of trade and commerce, does not have to come before parliament as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is doing now and ask that this measure be approved. I am sure that would be a little too embarrassing for him.
There are some aspects of this measure which have not worked too smoothly. The minister did not refer to them, so I should like to bring them to his attention so that consideration can be given to them before the bill is introduced.
First, I should like to ask him if the elevator companies have been consulted with regard to the higher cash advances that will be paid? Are they in agreement with this
DEBATES	813
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act idea? Second, it has become standard practice that a farmer can only have a cash advance once during a crop year. If a farmer has grain in storage, takes a cash advance on farm stored grain and then delivers grain to pay off that cash advance, even though he may have more grain on his farm he is prevented, for some reason or other, from taking another cash advance. I see no reason for this. If a farmer has paid off one cash advance why can he not take another? I should like the minister to consider this question because I think that provision has handicapped a number of farmers.
Another problem is related to the taking of cash advances on grain grown on rented or leased land. This has caused a great deal of trouble because in many cases the owner of the land is many miles away from the farm and it is very difficult to get his signature to a document granting permission for the farmer to sell the grain or take a cash advance on it. In my opinion the wheat board, the elevator companies and the government could work out a system whereby cash advances could be made on the farmer's share of the grain grown on rented land. I should like the minister to get together with representatives of the elevator companies to try to work out something along this line.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I should also like to say a few words about the farmers' ability to repay. If this resolution is accepted in its present form and the farmer may borrow up to $1 per bushel on his stored grain, then the very minute he delivers his wheat to the elevator company he has to pay back the advance he has received. If he is receiving at the delivery point only $1.50 a bushel, or $1.37 for No. 3 or $1.40, depending on where the delivery is made, and he has to deduct $1 a bushel for his cash advance, he will become more and more hesitant to deliver any grain. Therefore the payment will not necessarily be any great boost to the agricultural community.
I suggest that basically what the government should do is to allow the farmers to deliver their wheat as soon as possible, ensuring that there is a greater degree of even distribution throughout the prairie provinces. In the past couple of years there has been a great deal of difficulty in marketing grain, on one occasion because the railroads were reluctant to handle grain and wanted to haul potash instead. We have also seen in the past great interest on the part of the grain companies in storing low grades of wheat at the
October 4, 1968

Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act Lakehead, which has caused some points to have more storage space at the end of the year than others.
I want to leave this point with the minister. This legislation is not necessarily going to solve all our marketing problems. The government is going to advance to farmers another 50 cents per bushel on their own wheat, but this does not free the government from the responsibility of marketing wheat. I urge the Minister without Portfolio and the Minister of Trade and Commerce to get together and establish an objective for this year as to the amount of wheat they are going to sell abroad. This will instil greater confidence in the agricultural industry on the prairies in the ability of the government to market wheat.
Last year the farmers had a very poor delivery quota, the maximum being something like six bushels an acre. Let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that you cannot make a living growing wheat when you are allowed to sell only six bushels an acre, because it may cost as much as $2 an acre to spray for wild oats. It may also cost $1 an acre for fertilizer. Then there are all the other expenses, such as seeding and combining the grain. It costs over $3 an acre to combine grain, so how can a farmer operate with a six bushel quota?
The cash advance that is given to the farmer on his grain he has to repay eventually. The only way he can do this is to deliver his wheat, and he cannot deliver his wheat unless he has a sufficient quota and there is storage space at the elevator. If you follow the chain of reasoning, Mr. Chairman, it all goes back to the question of export sales.
It is interesting to note that about three weeks ago the United States government told U.S. farmers that they plan to export this year 750 million bushels. That is to be their target. Last year that was their target and in fact they exceeded it. This government has not got the intestinal fortitude, the confidence in itself or the initiative to say to the western farmers: We are with you; we will do our utmost to sell 450 million bushels of wheat this year. That is what the government should say. It is the duty of the government to give the farmers some hope of paying back the cash advances they will receive under this piece of legislation, instead of sitting on their hands with their mouths closed and saying that in three or even ten years perhaps they can sell a lot of grain.
[Mr. Horner.l
Under the cash advance legislation these loans have to be repaid in the year that the grain is delivered. Therefore I urge the Minister without Portfolio and the Minister of Trade and Commerce not to rest on their laurels because they are giving the farmers 50 cents more a bushel cash by way of advance. As I say, the farmer has to repay this sum when he delivers his grain. I urge these two ministers to go out and sell wheat and thus restore the confidence of the wheat growing industry of western Canada. This very industry has in the last five or six years bailed out the Canadian government from a lot of financial problems. Particularly during the last three or four years, our balance of payments problem was greatly relieved when Canadian exports of grain, mainly wheat, were stepped up to quite a large extent.
Therefore I leave with the minister this urgent plea. Let the government not be satisfied with a six bushel quota, as it was last year when the grain marketing year closed on July 31 last. Let the government tell the farmers that it will do its utmost to see that the quota is increased to at least eight, nine or possibly ten bushels. This is what the farmers want to hear and it will restore the confidence and way of life of this industry. I urge both ministers to restore that confidence because it is badly needed in this very important segment of our economy today.

Mr. Chairman, I have been long enough acquainted with the irrepressible member for Crowfoot to know that he has to have the last word. I certainly agree with the Minister without Portfolio that the proposal to increase the cash advance this year is in line with existing conditions under which grain is piling up on the prairies. Our farmers were short of cash before they went into this harvest season, let alone what their circumstances will be afterwards. Their situation has been complicated, of course, by bad weather. However, farmers have learned to live with different kinds of weather. If one were not prepared to suffer the consequences of weather, one would very soon cease to farm. The fact is that it is not so much the weather as the economic situation brought about by the present government and its administrative
October 4, 1968

policies which has caused the real difficulty for the fanners at this time.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The availability of farm credit should help to solve the farmers' difficulties, and the government has made a fair start in this legislation. Practically all the farm legislation we are considering at the moment is legislation having to do with credit, and the current piece of legislation we are now considering will be of advantage to our farmers. The money to be paid under this legislation does not bear interest and will not increase the cost of carrying a debt load. The farmer will still have that load but the cost of carrying it will not be increased.
All the same, this measure is strictly a temporary one. Any money the farmer borrows he must pay back as he delivers wheat and this, of course, brings us to the central question of our ability to market and sell his product. The wheat carryover this year is the highest since 1957, the year in which cash advances were initiated. It now stands at 733 million bushels of wheat.
The situation was aggravated to a considerable extent by the grain handlers' strike which tied up deliveries. The strike was allowed to go on far too long; fortunately it was settled eventually. The strike aggravated the problems inherent in slow marketing. At the same time, despite suggestions and requests made to the government the farmers will not be assisted in the building of grain storage facilities to handle the present crop. Instead, farmers will be forced to spend their own money or to borrow additional money in order to store grain. One may be sure that with a 733 million bushel carryover, a great deal of grain remains on farms.
If you go to my area of Saskatchewan and down the road to the east from my farm you will find a man who farms a section of 640 acres. This crop year all his granaries, with the exception of one small one, were filled with wheat. At another place farther down the road is another man who farms a section and a half, 960 acres. That man has grain from the previous year sitting in temporary storage. There is not point in mentioning names, but if you travel about the district you will find, a similar situation prevailing generally. These farmers are not large farmers when one compares them with others in western and central Saskatchewan but they must go out and buy granaries to store their grain, as I must. Out of our resources, out of
DEBATES	815
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act our savings, we must draw money to build storage facilities. This money is dead money; it is lost money because the storage bins are of value only for the storage of grain which cannot be sold. If anyone on the government side has the idea that the wheat economy of Saskatchewan can or will operate on a six bushel quota, he had better disabuse himself of this idea because it will not.
The corn growers came to stand in front of the parliament buildings in Ottawa. I tell you, sir, that if it were not for all the rock, bush, and water in the pre-Cambrian shield between here and Winnipeg, you would see just as many farmers from Saskatchewan driving their tractors here and standing on the front lawn.
I wish to impress on the house that this is a temporary piece of legislation; it solves the problem temporarily. I hope no one is lulled into the idea that our problems have been met and resolved. I do not blame the government for our slow wheat trade on the international market. Anyone can read the figures. I do, however, criticize the government for restricting some imports, and in this connection I shall mention an example. We restrict imports from Singapore. I read a press report saying that customs officials had put pressure on Singapore traders to force them to put "voluntary quotas on exports of cotton shirts and trousers," no doubt to protect the textile industry in Canada. That was the sort of method we used with the Japanese for years. The restrictions are not really voluntary. The quota on Japanese colour television sets has been cut back recently in order to allow the industry in Canada to compete effectively.
Sir, Japan is just behind England in being one of the largest buyers of Canadian wheat. Is this our way of increasing wheat sales? Is this how we want to encourage our wheat to move into the markets of the world? That sort of thing violates the spirit and the intention of some of our trade agreements. Is this the new look of the new society or is it simply the old protectionism of the thirties being updated and made to fit conditions in the 1960's. If we want to sell grain or other products we must make progress in the trade negotiations which have been going on.
Western farmers viewed with uneasiness the end of the international wheat agreement. The new international grains agreement still has to prove itself as being a workable instrument. Before the agreement came fully into force we saw what happened last year. The United States and two or three other competitors slashed prices, and it fell to us in Canada
October 4, 1968

Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act to bear the brunt of maintaining the existing price structure until the grains agreement could be signed. The western farmer paid the shot.
From my observation, I do not think any great progress was made in the GATT negotiations in breaking down barriers for agricultural products. I base my opinion on the observation that the restrictions on agricultural products entering the European Common Market remained practically the same as they were before. In the European Common Market agricultural products are subsidized and the market is protected against Canadian farm products. Our best chance at the moment appears to be in the Asian markets. I notice that the Australians have developed a brand new product for sale to the Indonesian market; they call it Rycena. Perhaps we should be doing more along these lines. I doubt whether we are moving fast enough at present.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
During the election campaign we heard about a proposal to recognize the People's Republic of China-I think that is the proper designation. This is what the grain growers out west, where I live, were told. However, now that the government is in office, I do not read in the press these days of any great haste about doing this. If anything is being done I shall be pleased to hear so. It is to this area we must look for the increased markets we need.
We are told by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce that we are to have a new national grains council, whatever that may be. I have seen press releases about it. The other day I asked the minister whether he would table the terms of reference and explain the purpose of the council, as well as give us the names of those who were to become members. As I read his reply in Hansard I understand he is ready to table the names of the members after they have been appointed. There is no mention of his attitude toward making known the terms of reference. I think it is important we should know the purpose of this proposed council and its terms of reference. In short, we should be told what it is for.
Over the years, indeed, practically speaking, during my lifetime, we have built up grain marketing machinery in western Canada largely as the result of the efforts of the farmers who live there and produce the grain. We have built the kind of marketing machinery which we thought was best suited to do
[Mr. Gleave.l
the job. We had a fair amount of trouble while doing so and we encountered some rough experiences. But out of it all we emerged with the Canadian Wheat Board, a staff who knew how to run it, the Board of Grain Commissioners, capable of controlling and overseeing the grain trade, and under them a staff of technical people well versed in the technical aspects of wheat marketing. More to the point, they are capable of handling wheat and grading it. Over the years we built up this system.
Within the Canadian Wheat Board we developed a staff with the knowledge and ability to sell wheat-and I know whereof I speak because I have sat with them overseas during two international negotiations. Certainly you cannot find more able men. We have people in the experimental service who know how to breed wheat and develop it. I wish we had more. I wish governments in the past had seen fit to provide money so that we did have more. No new variety of grain is approved unless these experimental people approve it and unless the Board of Grain Commissioners and the western grains standards committee give it approval. So if the sale of wheat is to be an imaginative, onward going process, there are already people with the brains and skill to do the job.
Now we are to have a national grains council. According to the last report I read, they are to meet in Winnipeg and consider then-terms of reference. These could be wide. If those terms of reference include wheat selling, pricing and so on, does the government intend to listen to the advice of the proposed national grains council or of the Canadian Wheat Board? Surely the time has come when the Minister of Trade and Commerce should answer fully the question I put to him in this house and tell us what the purpose of this grains council is to be. Like the trade policy of the government, like the foreign policy of the government, this will affect our well-being as wheat growers. Unless we do better than we have been doing, next year perhaps the Minister without Portfolio will be offering us loans of twice $6,000, that is $12,000. They have already gone up from three to six. Unless a better job is done he will be back with a worse problem next year, no doubt about it.
The farmers offered at one time to put up their own money for wheat utilization. The offer was not accepted, and I do not know why. In my experience in farm organization I do not recall many occasions when all the

unions and federations of agriculture in western Canada were completely agreed on one thing. On that occasion they were, but the offer was not accepted. What we really need are trained, expert people, men who are trained in our experimental and research systems, trained in the Wheat Board's selling techniques, equipped with the technical know-how which lies at the core of the Board of Grain Commissioners operations and which has always been available to government. If we marshal this skill and experience we will make progress. We do not need a lot more opinions. What we do need now is a fair bit of action.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on this occasion. First of all I want to congratulate my neighbour from the constituency to the west of my own upon having been appointed Minister without Portfolio, and upon having the opportunity to introduce legislation of this type. During the ten years that I have represented the people of my constituency I have recommended to them that they make the maximum use of this legislation. I have told them they should take advantage of the fact that the government of this country had faith in them and believed their grain would eventually be sold. This was primarily the thinking of the government in 1957 when it introduced the cash advance legislation. Up until the time that the Conservative government took office the attitude of the preceding government had been that it had no faith in the farmers' ability to sell their grain, and it did not believe cash advances should be paid to farmers for grain stored on their farms.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It is interesting to see the transformation over the years. I know the minister was quite sincere in his pleasure when introducing this legislation at this time. I note that over the last 11 years it has cost the treasury something like $7J million in order that farmers may derive benefit from this legislation, and not only the farmers but all business enterprises right down the line. I should like to say, in recalling the history of the great battle for cash advances which began in 1949 and took until 1957, that it is rewarding and satisfying to a number of hon. members to welcome the conversion of many people on the other side of the house. I would also like to say that I hope this will destroy the myth which was perpetrated in those days, and for the first year or two after cash advances were put into effect, that you could not trust the farmers, that if you paid them for some of the wheat which was in their granaries there was danger they might default on hauling to the grain elevators. The fact is that out of $450 million advanced in 11 years something in the neighbourhood of $45,000 was all that was short in terms of repayment. I submit that this record is unequalled in any section of our economy in the dealings of the people with their own government. People in the farm industry have always enjoyed a good reputation, and now they have established this good record which I think probably some other segments of our society could emulate.
One thing which I would hope all hon. members in all parties from areas other than the prairie provinces would tell the people in their respective constituencies is that cash advances on farmers' grain is not a subsidy or a gift. In too many urban centres, even in the odd place in the prairies and certainly in other parts of Canada, some people believe or have been given to understand that this is some sort of gift or subsidy to the agricultural industry. It most certainly is not. All it represents is an advance on the farmers' wages and earnings. No one in any other occupation would agree to receiving his pay once, twice or three times a year. I am sure that if members of this house were to get their indemnity cheques at Christmastime, next spring and when the house adjourned for the summer holidays, they would object loudly and would not stand for it.
Prior to the time of cash advances farmers had to put up with a lack of funds. This is not a subsidy, they are just getting what is rightly their due for their production. This 
provides them with an opportunity to get an advance, and when they finally deliver the wheat they receive the balance of the money that is due them after the cash advance has been deducted. As long as export grain sales are inadequate, as long as storage facilities both in the country and at the terminals are congested, and as long as railroads do not provide adequate rolling stock when there is space for grain movement, cash advances will be necessary under the law.
May I add to the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie in support of the greater use of the Hudson Bay route to the port of Churchill, that although his party had the unique opportunity of being the government of this country for six years and had the chance to implement the vision and use its imagination to really do something there, it passed up that chance. I do not think there is anyone in any political party in the three prairie provinces who does not favour and support the greater use of the Hudson Bay route.
It seems to me that here again is a matter which requires from a government, vision, imagination and courage the like of which no national government has yet shown. That is extremely kind, Mr. Speaker. I wonder with respect if, apropos of your remarks, I might argue with you that we are not dealing with revenues of the Crown or with lands of the Crown, because both the revenues and the lands referred to in the particular statute which I seek to repeal are held in trust, and I put those in a different class than being held directly. In any event, I am quite sure that even if the bill were one of those which fell within the class of being a money bill the government, with its tremendous concern for the rights and welfare of peoples, would have immediately come to my rescue, adopted it, and preceded it with the appropriate resolution.
However, I think that is all unnecessary, because if I remember the reading I did earlier about the history of the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act itself, the original bill in 1943 was not preceded by a resolution that dealt directly with the bill. In any event the house has been gracious enough to go along with your suggestion that we proceed without any argument about the formalities.
The year 1943, as I said earlier, was the year in which the parliament of Canada passed this law, and I suggest it was done in a relatively secret way and by collusion. I mean collusion in its worst sense, collusion between the then Liberal government here in Ottawa and the Liberal dominated coalition government in the province of British Columbia, because both governments were involved in working out an agreement which brought about the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act, which effectively removed from the native Indian people in B.C. the control that they might and would have otherwise have had of mineral resources whether upon or beneath Indian reserve land. This was done without any consultation with the native people, and done without their knowledge. I have asked many of the older people on reserves about this and none of them recall hearing anything at all, even about the passage of the law itself in 1943.
The origin of this question, I think, comes from the time when British Columbia entered confederation. One of the terms of the entering of my province was the building of a railroad, the C.P.R., and that railroad obtained a right of way some 40 miles in width. There can be great controversy and conversation about the propriety of having
October 4, 1968

done that, and about some of the subsequent changes, but nevertheless as a result of the C.P.R. obtaining a 40 mile swath of land along the length of the railway, as one of the considerations for its building the railroad, when gold was discovered in 1884 there came with it the question of the legislative or political control over the gold itself. In other words, was the proprietary ownership over the gold in the hands of the provincial government or in the hands of the then dominion government? As a consequence of this disagreement the matter went to litigation and subsequently ended up in the hands of the Privy Council who, in 1889, made a decision in effect that the precious metals on that particular land, which was railway right of way land, were declared to belong beneficially to the province.
In 1943 the then minister of mines and resources, hon. Mr. Crerar, introduced into parliament the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act, and I submit that he, for what reason I do not know, either misunderstood the decision of the Privy Council or misinterpreted it, and in effect made a court decision of the Privy Council, which was originally applied to land which had been given to a railway, apply to Indian reserve land. He added that because the Privy Council had made this decision with respect to the C.P.R. land, therefore we, the parliament of Canada, should have to pass a law endorsing in a legislative way the agreement between the British Columbia government and the Canadian government about mineral resources on Indian reserves.
I submit that there are two different questions involved here. I say that Mr. Crerar misapplied the finding of the Privy Council, and in effect by misapplying it, by misinterpreting it, in concert with the provincial government effectively took away-as has been the case in so many instances in the past- something more from the native Indian people of the province of British Columbia, namely the control over the mineral resources that might be on their lands.
Perhaps in this regard I might be permitted to quote from part of the decision of the Privy Council, which is to be found at page 306 of the Law Reports, Appeal Cases, 1889:
Their Lordships are for these reasons of the opinion that the judgment appealed from-
I might point out that the courts in Canada had made a decision in favour of the federal government or federal parliament.
-must be reversed, and that it ought to be declared that the precious metals within the rail-29180-53

The key words were "the precious metals within the railway belt." This is what the Privy Council was dealing with. They were not dealing with precious metals on Indian reserves, and I submit that this should clearly show that, to be gracious about it, at the very least there was great misunderstanding or lack of knowledge about the full effect of that decision, and that it should not have been applied to the precious metals on Indian reserves. This injustice has remained there ever since 1943, for the last 25 years, without any great or in any event successful attempt being made to correct the situation.
In 1966, Mr. Speaker, I introduced a bill with respect to this matter identical with that which is now before the house. In passing I might add that I think Your Honour was our presiding officer at that time, and no thoughts were expressed about the bill's being in order at that time. In any event, for 25 years now there has been this statutory injustice resting on the law books of Canada and on the books of the legislature in the province of British Columbia. This was done without consultation, without advice from or without considering any of the native people-in other words just a complete disregard for what we all fervently in our hearts believe to be a fundamental right of people, the right to be advised of what is taking place with regard to their respective rights.
I submit that in three instances the schedule to the act contains misleading information. Again, to substantiate what I say, that the government in 1943 consciously took action of a misleading nature to remove some of the fundamental rights of the Indian people, I point out that in a preliminary part the schedule reads as follows:
Whereas from time to time treaties have been made with the Indians for the surrender for various considerations of their personal and usufructury rights to territories now included in the province of British Columbia, such considerations including the setting apart for the exclusive use of the Indians of certain definite areas of land known as Indian reserves;
I submit that this was misleading because it contains within it the reference that "from time to time treaties have been made-"

That is the crux of the British Columbia land question. This was something that hon. Mr. Crerar knew about in 1943, and it was something that the government of that day knew about, because this B.C. land question has been before the parliament of Canada in one way or another as far back as the turn of the century. I submit that parts of the preamble indicate that the government knew this was misleading. Another part of the preamble states:
And whereas the said Indian reserves were conveyed to the dominion government as trustee for the Indians under the terms and conditions set forth in an agreement dated the 24th day of September, 1912, between the dominion government and the province of British Columbia;-
It is a well known fact, certainly to the Indian people and the government of that day, and the government of this day, that the native Indian people never at any time accepted the agreement of 1912 as a solution to the land problem. Nobody at that time accepted the finding of the McKenna-McBride royal commission which considered this question, and no one at any time accepted the decision of the Indian Land Settlement Acts that were passed by the legislature of British Columbia; and the native peoples have never signed any treaty. This in itself leaves the impression that the Indian people have agreed with this when in fact they have not. The third "whereas" which is misleading reads:
And whereas the precious metals in, upon, or under the lands comprising such reserves are not incidents of such lands but belong beneficially to the Crown in the right of the province of British Columbia with the result that the development of all the minerals in, upon or under such lands is at present impractical since the precious and base metals are closely associated and cannot be mined separately.
As I pointed out earlier, this is misleading because the decision of the Privy Council on this matter of precious metals had nothing whatever to do with the Indian lands in British Columbia, but dealt with lands ceded to the C.P.R. It should have been confined to that and not extended to take away the rights of our native people.
In 1965, three years ago, the Indian affairs branch submitted a directive which dealt with the matter of developing mineral

resources, which said that the only minerals that could be developed on reserves were those minerals that had been surrendered. It indicated that the minerals must be surrendered, and there is no equivocation about that. There is no maybe: They must be surrendered by the Indian people. In other words, the native Indian people, because of this British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act and the Indian Act, cannot participate in the development of resources on a reserve unless they first give them away, surrender them and relinquish all their rights and interests in them, in this instance to the Crown or the federal government.
In the first place this bill was an imposition as a result of some collusive agreement based upon a misinterpretation of the court decision. It was an imposition, and is a denial of fundamental rights of our Canadian native people to direct their own affairs and destinies. It is a denial of their right to local government in respect of their land and well being, and I suggest this should not be permitted to remain on the statute books of this nation. That is why I seek to repeal it.
Apart from the fundamentals, the directive to which I made reference earlier contained the reference that there has been increasing interest in mineral development in recent years, and certainly increasing interest in mineral development that might take place on Indian reserves. This British Columbia Indian Mineral Reserves Resources Act holds back or deters any such potential development because the native people are fed up to the teeth with having to give up their rights every time they want to obtain something. They are fed up with the concept of surrendering things. They are fed up with having to relinquish their authority and the control over reserve lands before anything can be developed. As a consequence they are not surrendering anything more, even though it might mean more income as a result of mineral development.
As I understand it, there are some agreements in the prairie provinces, the Maritime provinces and in Ontario which give to the native Indian people in those areas 100 per cent of the benefits resulting from any development of mineral resources on reserve land. With the concept of equality we should be moving toward this position and providing agreements of this type to the Canadian native Indians of British Columbia.

This is not the total amount that would accrue to the reserves, but is the production value. A great deal of this would accrue to the Indian people and we should keep that in mind. I know there are some who might argue at this juncture that the repeal of the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act may not be the right way to correct this situation, but my purpose at this time is to keep this matter alive and to foster a greater understanding of the injustice that was perpetrated and has remained uncorrected. In view of the government's desire to make our committees function to a greater extent I hope that the appropriate minister, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) or the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras), will concern themselves with this matter and refer it to a committee for study. In this way the Canadian native Indian people could be given the opportunity to present their ideas. They could be consulted and their feelings could be ascertained in respect of this particular act.
Many consultations are taking place in this country with the native Indian people about the Indian Act. Mr. Speaker, I hope that this matter will be taken to the level of immediately active advisement rather than just the immediate advisement stage. We are beginning to learn that there are differentiations in the government's approach to problems. We hope this bill will receive the urgent treatment which it deserves.
I certainly support the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) in his proposals. I was a member of the Indian affairs committee some years ago when this matter, amongst others, was raised. I have some recollection of it and I have here the act which the hon. member seeks to have repealed. I might say in passing that the hon. member for Skeena referred to the fact that this was a case where there was no consultation with the
October 4, 1968
832	COMMONS
B.C. Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act Indians. It is a sad commentary on the government of this country that for a period of 25 years we see the same course of action pursued.
This house was agitated, as it properly should have been, last week, and to some extent it has been this week, by charges made, and never refuted, that the Indian people of this country were not consulted on a very, very important reorganization of the Indian affairs department with regard to a matter in which the Indians were involved and definitely concerned. The only occasion I can recall when there was a real measure of consultation was during the course of the administration of the Conservative government from 1957 to 1963.
The Indian affairs committee was set up. One hundred witnesses were called, including a very large number of representatives of the Indian people from all over Canada. These people were brought here and gave evidence which was uninhibited in any respect. We received a great deal of very useful information. The committee made recommendations. Some of them were initiated before the Conservative government fell, but have not been dealt with since. I must say in passing that here we are, 25 years later, and the same charges are still being made against the government by the same people. These charges are of the same political nature, namely that they are not being consulted when they should be.
I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker. Reading the act, I agree with the hon. member that there are three assumptions drawn in the preamble which I think are incorrect. It is in fact a creation of a statutory image, a statutory illusion, not based on truth and not based on the facts. I shall deal with only the first of these assumptions. The following words are to be found in the preamble:
-from time to time treaties have been made with the Indians for the surrender for various considerations of their personal and usufructury rights-
This has been repeated over and over again. A number of treaties were entered into with Indian people and Indian bands by which it was sought to acquire the title of the Indian people to practically all the lands between the Great Lakes and the Rocky mountains and extending into the Northwest Territories. These treaties were similar to the one to which the hon. member for Skeena has referred. They were based on certain considerations. Letters were executed by the commissioners who drew up these treaties. The


letters detailed the circumstances under which the treaties were made. There is no question at all that, as in this case, the Indian people were led to believe that in surrendering their rights-the complete extent of which was probably not known to them-they would be given certain other considerations. Some very definite considerations were put forward to the Indian people as being given to them in exchange for their giving away these rights.
We all know the famous case which went before the Supreme Court of Canada. I refer to the lame duck case. In that case the Supreme Court of Canada held that because of the Migratory Birds Convention Act certain rights to which the Indian people felt they were entitled with regard to hunting, trapping and fishing, were not to be given to them because the federal government, one of the parties to the treaties with the Indians, was in direct violation of the undertaking in that the treaty entered into internationally imposed obligations upon the federal government which the Supreme Court of Canada held to have precedence over the treaties with the Indians.
There are a number of other cases of this type. There was the so-called medicine chest case. In a number of these treaties there was a provision that the government would provide certain medical and other services within the meaning of the words medicine chest, which to the Indian people at that time had a very specific and special connotation. This was another case where the federal government, through its counsel, intervened. But I do not think any real, conscious effort has been made by this government to in any way right the wrong that has been done to the Indian people by the violation of their treaty rights.
For these general reasons, in addition to the specific reasons to which the hon. member for Skeena has referred, I hope that this matter will be referred to a committee. I certainly hope that when the Indian claims commission legislation is introduced, this issue will be given the most serious thought.
We have done injustices to the Indian people. There is no use cataloguing the litany of evils, wrongs and misdemeanours which have been committed. This is now a matter of history. But there is now probably the last opportunity, through the medium of legislative proposals which I suppose this government will introduce, to widen the extent of
October 4, 1968	COMMONS
those proposals to include the kind of compensation to which the Indian people are entitled. This we must do if we are to hold up our heads and say we have kept the sacred obligations which previous governments entered into on behalf of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) upon raising this subject, and I have listened with great interest to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). I do not suppose anybody in this house is not in sympathy with the spirit behind the words of both hon. gentlemen. I hope no members of the house will be out of sympathy with the words I shall be using. I might as well state at the outset that I do not feel this bill should be dealt with as a separate and individual item. I think it is an excellent idea that it be referred to the committee, as a specific item to be looked at in the context of the whole question.
To arrive at that conclusion I think one has to realize that we are, in a sense, at the apex of 300 years of injustice which we and our forefathers have perpetrated on the Indians. We are just arriving at a time when a fundamental change can probably be made, and the Indians are just getting back their self confidence to a sufficient degree to be able to help themselves. When the white man first came to Canada he was prone to think of the Indians as mysterious creatures flitting around among the trees and in the distance, people whom no one understood. It has become more and more apparent, thanks to studies of historians such as Mclnnes and others, that the Indians had a viable, sensible and economic way of life supported by a good system of trade. If you look back at the efforts of the French pioneers, you will find that they did not do what later generations did, but that they tried to establish trading and leave the Indians basically undisturbed. Unfortunately their idea of trade included brandy, which did harm to many Indians, but that was not a deliberate policy.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The Indians still staked off their own territory, the Algonquins in one place and the Iroquois in another. Some were farmers, some were traders and some were middlemen. All this change started taking place in Canada only a little more than 100 years ago. In the United States this was started a little earlier when people, actually, physically took possession of the land. I suggest this is where the trouble started which led to the situation
DEBATES	833
B.C. Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act of the Indian today. Louis Riel saw this, and in drawing up and passing the Manitoba act he attempted to stop this from happening in Manitoba and in the west. However, the white people reneged on the deal they made with the natives in my province, and as a result the Indians and Metis were the ones to suffer. I am glad to see that the position of the Indians is now being seen in better perspective and that it is recognized that Louis Riel was trying to achieve something serious.
It was at that time that reserves were set aside to be administered by the Crown on behalf of the Indians, and 1,400,000 acres was made available to the Metis, But the Indians were unable to make a living off the reserve and the Metis lands were soon in the hands of speculators. So the Metis are in as much trouble as are the Indians, and I hope they will not be forgotten when the time comes.
Between 1871 and 1877, seven treaties were negotiated between Canada and the Indians of the new Northwest. It is quite obvious that the Indians thought, as the hon. member intimated, that they were making a perfectly genuine deal with a trustworthy partner. To prove this I would like to quote the words of the Lac Seul chief in connection with the signing of treaty No. 3. This is what he said:
We are the first that were planted here. We would ask you to assist us with every kind of implement to use for our benefit... a little of everything, and money. We would borrow your cattle; . .. the waters out of which you sometimes take food for yourselves, we wll lend you in return . . . The time may come when I will ask you to lend me one of your daughters and one of your sons to live with us; and in return I will lend you one of my daughters and one of my sons for you to teach what is good, and after they have learned, to teach us.
The key words there are obviously share, exchange and lend. That is what treaty No. 3 was all about so far as the Lac Seul chief knew. He found out differently later. I suggest that all the treaties were like this one. The last time that the Indians tried seriously to improve their lot was when they threw in their weight behind Louis Riel in 1885. This became a rebellion which was put down, and that was the end of that.
I suggest that the treaty to which the hon. member for Skeena referred was a little different. The spirit behind it, so far as the dominion government was concerned, was the same, and it proved to be just as much of a failure, but the mechanics were a little different because British Columbia came in as a separate colony.

speechtext:
This is what I was about to say. I thank the hon. member for making it clear that I am not being clear. British Columbia was a separate Crown colony. No treaties were made but there was a general indication that the same spirit prevailed because when British Columbia joined confederation it negotiated its own terms. Although the dominion took charge of Indian affairs, the province would have to give it whatever lands it required for reservations. That was part of the act under which that province came in.
It is clear from the terms of union that the federal authorities thought they were following through with the same pattern they had established toward Indians in the rest of western Canada. Land would be given to them to be held in trust, for the use and benefit of Indians in British Columbia. But when the time came to actually select this land, trouble occurred. Commissions had to be set up, either jointly or unilaterally, by the two governments involved. It was not until 1938 that by provincial order in council reserves were conveyed to the dominion, and a time span of 67 years had elapsed. So I think there is a very good indication that the spirit of the law was not lived up to.
Meanwhile, in 1889, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to which the hon. member referred ruled that precious metals were vested in the province. Later the province made claim for the administration of base metals. So they tried to get the whole lot. The British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act passed in 1943 was an attempt to regularize the situation. The administration, control and disposal of all minerals and mineral claims on Indian reserves in British Columbia was made subject to the laws of the province, and all revenues arising out of the sale or royalty agreements would be split henceforth between the federal and the provincial governments on a 50-50 basis. This settled nothing so far as the Indians were concerned, except to place the administration respecting precious and non-precious metals, under one roof. This might have been a good thing if there had been any will to do so for the benefit of the Indians.
Notwithstanding the foregoing arrangement, under the present act when a band approves a mineral surrender, which it still has to approve, the administrative responsibility is immediately split. The band has jurisdiction over the surface rights, the province has jurisdiction over the mineral rights, and no one has yet discovered how the devil one can get close to the minerals without disturbing the land rights. The jurisdiction is divided and diffuse. I suggest that this is a very good reason that there has been no significant development of the potential mines on British Columbia Indian land. Who would ever make a deal with anyone when they do not know how to get to the minerals, how to mine them and whom to negotiate the terms with?
Both the federal and the provincial authorities realize this is a poor arrangement. Through the years there have been discussions between the province and the federal government is respect of the interpretation or this act. These discussions have altered the conditions slightly in favour of the Indians, but have not resulted in serious exploration or development. As of this date the province has advised the federal government that changes in the act could not be considered.
So the Indians sit and wait for the white man to unscramble the mess. How is it possible to get at the treasures underground without disturbing the land above? How is it possible to find a sensible method of exploiting the riches of nature for the benefit of the Indians without setting the province and the federal authorities at loggerheads one with another? To the Indians, who so desperately need all the revenue they can lay their hands on, this must seem like a very sorry state of affairs. It would be funny if it were not so sad.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Now, having said this, I should like to submit that I have not cited an isolated case. This is an example of the shocking way in which we, as white men, have treated the Indians. I do believe that the climate is such this government is going to be forced to take a serious look at the situation and really open the way for the Indian to help himself. If this is the case, then I submit we should not consider this bill in isolation, but it should be referred to the committee and considered in the context of the whole problem.

So far as I am concerned, an Indian or the average citizen of Canada cannot afford to litigate in the Exchequer Court. First of all, in order to get into the court he has to go to Ottawa, so he has to hire a lawyer in Ottawa, who is generally an agent of the legal firm of the place in which the person resides. For example, the Indians on the Blackfoot reserve have a claim in connection with their oil rights. They go to a lawyer in Calgary, and the Calgary lawyer communicates with a legal firm in Ottawa which, in turn, goes to the Exchequer Court. A poor man or an Indian cannot afford to do this.
