speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by complimenting the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) upon his very eloquent plea on behalf of the Indian people of Canada. In this one aspect at least, this hon. member and I share a great concern. It may be somewhat unusual for the member for Thunder Bay to rise to speak on a matter that concerns the Indian people of British Columbia; however, a great many of the constituents of Thunder Bay are native citizens of Canada. My interest in them and my concern for them leads me to be sympathetic toward Indian people, regardless of the corner of this land in which they happen to dwell.
It has been my privilege, Mr. Speaker, on at least one occasion to be present during the consultations the government has been having with the Indian people of Canada. I wish to testify to this house and to the people of Canada that these consultations with the Indian people were open, forthright confrontations. I should like to make it clear also that if any member of this house in any way casts suspicion upon the motives behind these consultations, he is doing a great disservice to the government and to the Indian people of Canada. The people attending these consultations have expressed their grievances well. It is the intention of the government, when all the data is available, to take the appropriate action, having listened carefully to what the Indian people have had to say.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
With reference to the situation in British Columbia, for many decades now there has been a great deal of concern as to who owns the minerals which reside under Indian reserves, and as to how they may best be developed. The real problem here is that there has been so little development and exploration of the minerals in these Indian reserves that it is to fog the issue for us to say that this act ought to be repealed. The real point is that the Indian people living on reserves in British Columbia have not profited economically from the resources which lie beneath the land on which they live.
It has been recommended, Mr. Speaker, that reference be made to the courts to determine ownership of these Indian resources. I suppose there are some pretty good legal arguments to suport the beneficial Indian right
[Mr. Woolliams.1

to precious metals, although a court judgment gives the ownership to the province. There is no justification for the provincial claim to ownership of base metals on Indian reserves.
Reference to the courts to determine ownership of British Columbia Indian resources will not contribute toward reaching an effective agreement on the development of minerals on Indian reserves. In the last analysis, we want some benefit to accrue to the Indian people. We do not want the matter to become bogged down in long legal haggles in the courts of Canada. There are some good legal arguments which can certainly be helpful in demonstrating to the province of British Columbia that there is a strong case for Indian ownership. The act of 1943 implies that the province acquires administration of the minerals on Indian lands, and 50 per cent of the revenues, on the basis of the provincial right to the gold and silver. This basis is no longer a valid one. Although in 1940 the value of gold and silver amounted to 43 per cent of the value of all metals produced in the province, by 1966 gold and silver had declined to only 6 per cent of the metal production. By giving up administrative control of the minerals on Indian reserves, loss in revenue to the province from fees for recording claims and assessment work would be negligible, and may be more than offset by reduced administrative costs.
Indians in British Columbia should have the very same benefits from the development of their minerals as those enjoyed by Indians in other provinces. Agreements in effect in the prairie provinces and the maritime provinces, and one now being concluded in Ontario, provide full benefit for the Indian bands from development under federal administration of the minerals on their reserves. Indian affairs policy now provides for the Indian band councils to retain a large measure of control over the development of their mineral resources and to participate in the management functions. Under present provincial administration and legislation in British Columbia, Indian band council control over the minerals is both indirect and ineffective. I recommend, Mr. Speaker, that strong representations be made by the federal government, with of course support from the Indians of British Columbia, to the government of British Columbia for a new agreement for development of mineral resources on Indian reserves. This new agreement, moreover, should be patterned after the agreement
October 4, 1968
COMMONS DEBATES	837
B.C. Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act
now being concluded with Ontario and should contain the following provisions:
First, that British Columbia transfer to Canada control and administration of all mineral resources in Indian reserve lands or surrendered Indian lands, and the proceeds of the leases or other dispositions of the mineral resources be applied for the benefit of the Indians for whose use and benefit the said lands were set apart;
Second, that royalties paid for the benefit of Indians from minerals produced on the Indian lands shall, for the purposes of any provincial mining tax, be deductible from the income of the producer of the minerals;
Third, that the province agree to provide for technical surveys, safety measures and other similar services related to the exploitation of minerals on Indian lands that are normally provided for other lands in the province.
There would be a great deal of potential for the economic well-being of the Indian people of British Columbia if this policy were to be adopted, Mr. Speaker. For example, we know that there is an area of about 800,000 acres which is divided into 1,600 separate reserves spread over the province. The value of the minerals in this area is very difficult to assess, owing to their nature; the resources are hidden below the earth's surface.
Assuming for a moment that the average acre of Indian land has the same potential as the average acre of land within the province, the potential value of mineral production
from these lands may be estimated from the total mineral production of the province. The value of the metal production alone was worth over $200 million in 1966, or about $1 per acre. Applying this average to the 800,000 acres of Indian land, an annual production from the Indian lands of $800,000 may be expected. At the present time no metals are produced. The point, Mr. Speaker, is that economic benefits must accrue to the Indian people so that with their own resources they can develop a way of life suitable to them and that is designed particularly by them.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we admit that there are a great many difficulties in the present situation. Since the effective date of the act in 1943, mineral surrenders to only eight reserves out of a total of 1,600 reserves in British Columbia have been approved by Indian bands. Administrative responsibility for the use of the land resources is divided between the two governments, once a band has approved a mineral surrender. The mining or subsurface rights is administered by the British Columbia government, whereas the rights to use land surface for mining purposes are administered by the federal government, in consultation with the band council.
